This is only a reweighted observed contrast: causal interpretation needs conditional exchangeability, correct propensity models, and overlap. A propensity near 0.95 would give a comparison weight of 19, so one observation could dominate; inspect weight distributions and consider a pre-specified trim, recognizing that trimming changes the represented applicant population.
matching-weighting.The propensity score is a balancing summ: Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four households have estimated participation scores e of 0.25, 0.75, 0.25 and 0.75. The first two received the voucher and recorded 8 and 10 months housed; the latter two did not and recorded 5 and 7 months. For an inverse-probability-weighted ATE, assign treated weight 1/e and control weight 1/(1−e): the treated weights are 4 and 1.333, while the control weights are 1.333 and 4. Normalize within arm rather than comparing raw weighted sums. The weighted treated mean is (4×8 + 1.333×10)/(4 + 1.333) = 8.50 months, and the weighted control mean is (1.333×5 + 4×7)/(1.333 + 4) = 6.50 months; the estimated contrast is therefore 2.00 months. This calculation targets the combined population represented by the ATE weights, not necessarily the treated group. It is only illustrative, not observed data: credible interpretation still requires correctly specified pre-treatment scores, positivity, and no unmeasured confounding. A score near 0 or 1 would create a large weight, so inspect overlap and consider whether trimming changes the target before trusting precision.
matching-weighting.Check overlap and balance: Consider a different illustrative, synthetic diagnostic for pre-program rent burden, measured in percentage points of monthly income. Suppose the treated mean is 52 and the comparison mean is 44; assume each group’s SD is 10 and 14 percentage points. Using the simple pooled-SD approximation, the denominator is sqrt((10² + 14²)/2) = sqrt(148) = 12.17 percentage points, so the standardized mean difference is (52 − 44)/12.17 = +0.66 SD units. After reweighting, suppose the means become 49 and 48 while these illustrative SDs remain 10 and 14: the new SMD is (49 − 48)/12.17 = +0.08 SD units. The movement toward zero is evidence that this measured covariate is more comparable, not evidence that voucher assignment is as-good-as-random. Before interpreting the improvement, inspect whether the weights concentrate on a few households and whether the treated and comparison rent-burden distributions actually overlap; similar means can hide separated tails. Also state whether the weighting targets the treated population, the combined sample, or another population, because the same reweighting can change the estimand. The pooled-SD shortcut is a summary choice, not a universal balance threshold.
matching-weighting.State the assumptions and target: For a treated-population (ATT) estimand, inverse-odds weighting can make the untreated group resemble the treated group on measured covariates. Illustrative synthetic example: give each treated household weight 1, and give an untreated household with estimated propensity score e the weight e/(1−e). Suppose three untreated households have rent-burden outcomes of 6, 9, and 11 percentage points and scores 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75; their weights are 1/3, 1, and 3. The weighted untreated mean is [(1/3)×6 + 1×9 + 3×11] / [(1/3)+1+3] = 44/4.333… = 10.15 percentage points. If the three treated households’ mean is 12.00 percentage points, the weighted ATT contrast is 12.00 − 10.15 = 1.85 percentage points, interpreted for treated households—not all eligible households. Before trusting it, inspect covariate balance and common support, because a score near 1 creates a large control weight; here the weight 3 already makes one observation influential. The calculation still relies on conditional exchangeability and correctly specified scores; neither is established by balance alone.
matching-weighting.Weighting choices define which populatio: A useful stability check is the effective sample size (ESS), calculated after choosing the target population. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four comparison households receive normalized weights 1, 1, 2, and 4 to represent the treated target. The total weight is 8, and the sum of squared weights is 1² + 1² + 2² + 4² = 22, so ESS = (Σw)²/Σw² = 8²/22 = 64/22 ≈ 2.91 households. Although four households appear in the weighted calculation, their unequal influence gives precision closer to roughly three equally weighted observations, not four; the ESS is a diagnostic, not a literal replacement sample. Multiplying every weight by the same constant leaves a normalized weighted mean unchanged and also leaves this ESS unchanged, because the scale cancels. By contrast, trimming the weight of the fourth household would usually raise ESS while excluding or down-weighting part of the target population. An analyst should therefore report the weighting rule, retained overlap, ESS, and whether the estimand is ATT, ATE, or another explicitly defined target. Even a comfortable ESS cannot address unmeasured confounding or justify extrapolation beyond common support.

synthetic-control.Construct a comparison from donor units: To diagnose whether a reported gap is large relative to construction error, compute pre-policy RMSPE (root mean squared prediction error) before interpreting the post-policy path. Illustrative synthetic values: across four pre-policy periods, treated outcomes are 10, 12, 11, and 13 outcome units, while the synthetic series is 10.2, 11.8, 11.3, and 12.7. The errors are −0.2, 0.2, −0.3, and 0.3 units; squaring gives 0.04, 0.04, 0.09, and 0.09, whose mean is 0.065, so RMSPE = √0.065 ≈ 0.255 outcome units. If the three post-policy gaps are 1.0, 1.3, and 1.1 units, their average gap is 1.13 units, about 1.13 ÷ 0.255 ≈ 4.4 times the pre-policy RMSPE. That ratio flags a visually substantial departure in this teaching example, but it is not a p-value or proof of an effect. Re-estimate after excluding each influential donor, and compare the treated ratio with analogous ratios from placebo-treated donors; concurrent policies or a poorly chosen donor pool can still explain the divergence.
synthetic-control.Pre-treatment fit is the first check: Illustrative calculation (synthetic values, not observed data): suppose a treated region and its weighted donor combination have four pre-policy gaps, defined as treated minus synthetic outcome, of +0.20, −0.10, +0.30, and 0.00 jobs per 1,000 residents. The root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE) is sqrt[(0.20² + (−0.10)² + 0.30² + 0.00²) / 4] = sqrt(0.035) ≈ 0.187 jobs per 1,000 residents. If the average post-policy gap over two periods is +1.20 jobs per 1,000, the descriptive post/pre ratio is 1.20 / 0.187 ≈ 6.4. This ratio says the post-policy divergence is large relative to the model’s typical pre-policy discrepancy; it is not a p-value, confidence interval, or causal effect. First verify that the pre-period gaps do not show a systematic trend, then check whether one donor supplies most of the weight and recompute the diagnostic after excluding it. A ratio can look impressive when pre-fit is almost perfect, so report the raw post-policy gap and its units as well. The interpretation still requires unaffected donors, no anticipation or spillovers, and no concurrent shock that selectively changes the treated region.
synthetic-control.Inspect donors and modelling choices: Use a fit-scaled placebo check before treating a large gap as persuasive. Suppose, purely illustratively, a treated country’s pre-policy emissions gaps from its synthetic control (in million tonnes of CO₂ per year) are +0.2, −0.1, +0.3, and −0.2. The pre-period RMSPE is √[(0.2²+0.1²+0.3²+0.2²)/4] = √0.045 ≈ 0.21 million tonnes per year. If the three post-policy gaps are +1.1, +1.0, and +1.3, the post RMSPE is √[(1.1²+1.0²+1.3²)/3] = √1.30 ≈ 1.14 million tonnes per year, so the post/pre ratio is 1.14/0.21 ≈ 5.4. Next, reassign the intervention label to each eligible donor and calculate the same ratio, using the identical pre- and post-period definitions. A treated ratio of 5.4 is more informative if most placebo ratios are near 1, but it is not a p-value and does not establish causality. Discarding poorly fitting placebos can make the ranking look stronger, so set a transparent pre-fit rule in advance; also report the raw gaps because a high ratio can result from an unusually tiny denominator.
synthetic-control.Use placebos as a reference, not a magic: A useful refinement is to scale each unit’s post-policy discrepancy by its own pre-policy root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE), so a large raw gap is not mistaken for an unusual change when the synthetic match was already poor. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the treated unit has pre-policy RMSPE 0.5 outcome units and post-policy RMSPE 2.0 outcome units; its deterioration ratio is 2.0 ÷ 0.5 = 4.0. Compute the same ratio for every placebo using the identical pre- and post-period windows. If the placebo ratios are 1.2, 1.8, 2.6, and 5.0, the treated ratio exceeds three of four, but not the largest; that is a descriptive rank, not a probability that the policy worked. Before ranking, inspect whether any denominator is near zero, because tiny pre-fit error can make a modest post-gap look enormous. Also report the raw outcome-unit gap alongside the ratio: scaling improves comparability, but it cannot repair donor contamination, anticipation, or a structurally different treated unit.
synthetic-control.Compare placebo units only when their pr: A useful second diagnostic is to scale each post-policy gap by that unit’s own pre-policy root mean squared gap, rather than ranking raw gaps alone. Use the ratio R = |post-policy gap| / pre-policy RMS gap; the numerator and denominator are both in outcome units, so R is unit-free. Illustrative synthetic values make the calculation concrete: suppose the treated region’s gap is 1.20 outcome units and its pre-policy RMS gap is 0.30, giving R_T = 1.20 / 0.30 = 4.00. A placebo region with a 0.90-unit gap but a 0.30-unit pre-fit error has R_P = 3.00, whereas another with a 1.00-unit gap and 0.80-unit pre-fit error has R_P = 1.25. The raw gaps alone would make the latter look more unusual; the scaled ratios reverse that impression because its baseline mismatch was larger. Treat this as a descriptive diagnostic, not a p-value or causal proof. If a pre-fit RMS gap is zero or extremely small, the ratio becomes undefined or unstable; report the raw gap too and use a pre-specified minimum denominator or a separate sensitivity analysis.

limited-outcomes.Start with the outcome’s support: A probability-scale slope and a logit-index slope must be translated before they can be compared. Illustrative synthetic example: take a baseline placement probability of 40% at predictor index x = 0. With an LPM slope of 0.12, moving to x = 1 gives 0.40 + 0.12(1) = 0.52, a 12 percentage-point increase; moving to x = −2 gives 0.16, still inside [0,1] for this range. For a logit with the same 40% baseline and index slope 0.80, first compute the baseline log-odds log(0.40/0.60) ≈ −0.405. At x = 1 the index is −0.405 + 0.80 = 0.395, so the predicted probability is 1/[1 + exp(−0.395)] ≈ 0.597, or 59.7%. The comparable change from x = 0 is therefore about 19.7 percentage points, not 0.80 points. Because the logit effect varies with baseline risk, report predicted probabilities or marginal effects at relevant x values. Also check the whole policy-relevant range: an LPM can leave [0,1] outside the plotted range, while a logit stays bounded; neither calculation alone establishes a causal placement effect without a credible design.
limited-outcomes.Compare linear probability and nonlinear: To turn a nonlinear-link coefficient into a local probability statement, differentiate the inverse-logit rather than multiplying the coefficient by 100. Illustrative synthetic calculation using the lab’s default settings: let the baseline probability at predictor index x = 0 be p = 0.40 and let the logit index slope be β = 0.80 per index unit. The local marginal effect at x = 0 is p(1 − p)β = 0.40 × 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.192 probability units per index unit, or 19.2 percentage points per one-unit increase, holding the other covariates and outcome horizon fixed. This is a local derivative, not a universal effect: evaluating the same curve gives p(−1) = 23.1% and p(1) = 59.7%, so moving from −1 to 1 changes the prediction by 36.7 percentage points, not 2 × 19.2 = 38.4 points. The difference arises because the logistic curve flattens near zero and one. The contrast remains a model-based conditional association unless a credible assignment design supports a causal interpretation; report the covariate values and horizon with any marginal effect.
limited-outcomes.Choose a count model and inspect its lim: When people are observed for different lengths of time, compare rates rather than raw counts. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a comparison group averages 3 appointments during 6 person-months of eligibility, giving a rate of 3 ÷ 6 = 0.50 appointments per person-month. A Poisson specification can write E[Y_i|X_i,t_i] = t_i exp(X_iβ), or equivalently include log(t_i) as a fixed offset. If an appointment-system indicator has β = 0.20, its rate ratio is exp(0.20) ≈ 1.221, so the modeled rate is about 22.1% higher—not 0.20 additional appointments and not a 20-percentage-point probability change. Holding exposure at six person-months, the illustrative expected count changes from 6(0.50) = 3.00 to 3.00 × 1.221 ≈ 3.66 appointments; this is an expectation, not a guarantee for an individual. Before interpreting it, verify that eligibility time is measured consistently, that the offset is not itself affected by the system, and that residual dispersion or dependence does not make Poisson uncertainty misleading. The rate ratio remains associational unless a credible design supports a causal reading.
limited-outcomes.Censoring and selection need different s: Consider an illustrative synthetic labor-market file with a 12-month follow-up. For a worker who finds a job in month 5, the unemployment duration is recorded as 5 months; for one still unemployed at month 12, the record says 12+ months. The second value is right-censored, not evidence that the spell ended at 12, so a survival analysis should retain that worker’s 12 months at risk and mark the event as unobserved. In a separate wage file, suppose wages are observed only for the 6 of 10 synthetic workers who accepted a job. The four missing wages are not censored wages at a known ceiling: their values are unobserved because employment selection occurred. First define the estimand—time to re-employment for the full worker population or mean wage among employed workers—then ask whether the recording rule is administrative censoring or outcome-dependent observation. A model for censored duration and a selection model answer different questions; neither becomes causal merely because its likelihood fits. Report the follow-up horizon, event definition, and who could enter the wage sample.
limited-outcomes.Translate nonlinear coefficients onto th: A useful diagnostic is to separate a local marginal effect from a finite change in a predictor. Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic logit model with log-odds index η = −0.4055 + 0.8x; the intercept is −0.4055 because at x = 0 the baseline probability is 0.40, since ln(0.40/0.60) ≈ −0.4055. The derivative is ∂p/∂x = p(1−p)·0.8, so at x = 0 it equals 0.40×0.60×0.8 = 0.192, or about 19.2 percentage points for a one-unit change locally. That is not the exact effect over a wide move: at x = 1, p = 1/[1+exp(−(−0.4055+0.8))] ≈ 0.597, so moving from x = 0 to x = 1 changes probability by 0.597−0.400 = 0.197, or 19.7 percentage points. At x = −1, p ≈ 0.230, showing why the same coefficient does not imply the same probability change everywhere. These calculations assume the covariate comparison and functional form are meaningful; they describe model predictions, not a causal effect without credible assignment or adjustment.

selection-missing-data.Missing rows can change the question: Use the attrition check to separate an observed contrast from a sensitivity scenario. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose 250 people are assigned an offer and 250 a comparison condition; 20% of the offer group and 10% of the comparison group lack follow-up, so the observed means describe 200 and 225 people, not the original 250-person groups. If the observed outcome gap (offer minus comparison) is +2.0 units, do not silently call it the assignment effect. In the lab’s deliberately simplified scenario, let the unobserved offer-group outcomes be 1.5 units lower than the corresponding unobserved comparison outcomes. The sensitivity adjustment is (1 − 0.20) × (−1.5) = −1.20 units, giving an adjusted gap of 2.00 − 1.20 = +0.80 units. This is not a recovered truth: it is conditional on the chosen shift and the lab’s one-sided adjustment, while comparison attrition still warrants inspection. Report assignment counts, observed counts, attrition rates, and the range of plausible shifts; identification would require stronger assumptions or a design addressing differential follow-up.
selection-missing-data.State the missingness assumption: Illustrative synthetic sensitivity check: suppose 100 people are offered training and 100 are in the comparison group. Offer-group attrition is 20%, so 80 offer outcomes are observed; comparison attrition is 10%, so 90 comparison outcomes are observed. If the observed monthly earnings means are £54 and £50, the complete-case gap is £4 per month, but reconstructing the assigned-group means requires assumptions about the 30 missing earnings values. Set the comparison missing mean to £50 and let the offer missing mean be £50 + δ, where δ is the assumed offer-minus-comparison difference among missing people. The all-assigned gap is [(80×54 + 20×(50+δ)) − (90×50 + 10×50)] ÷ 100 = £3.20 + 0.20δ per month. Thus δ = −£10 gives £1.20, δ = £0 gives £3.20, and δ = £10 gives £5.20. This range is a sensitivity analysis, not a discovered effect: it changes the estimand from observed responders to everyone assigned and depends on plausible missing-outcome values. Random assignment could support a causal offer effect only with appropriate design and interpretation; attrition assumptions remain central.
selection-missing-data.Account for selective observation: Consider a synthetic job-training follow-up with 200 people offered training and 200 comparison people. Among offer-group responders, mean monthly earnings are $2,200; among comparison responders, they are $2,000. Response rates are 85% and 70%, respectively, so the complete-case gap is $200 per month, but that is not automatically the effect for everyone assigned. For a transparent sensitivity calculation, suppose comparison-group nonresponders would average the observed comparison mean, $2,000, and let δ be the offer-group nonresponder mean minus $2,000. The offer-group population mean under this scenario is 0.85($2,200) + 0.15($2,000 + δ) = $2,170 + 0.15δ, while the comparison mean is $2,000; hence the adjusted contrast is $170 + 0.15δ per month. If δ = $400, the contrast is $230; if δ = −$400, it is $110. These are illustrative synthetic assumptions, not recovered outcomes. Report the response rates, denominator, and δ range explicitly: if plausible values cross zero or reverse the conclusion, the result is sensitive to attrition rather than securely identified.
selection-missing-data.Show sensitivity and preserve denominato: A different check is to standardize observed outcomes to the baseline mix that was assigned, rather than letting differential follow-up redefine the target population. Illustrative synthetic example: each arm starts with 120 people, two-thirds in a lower-risk stratum and one-third in a higher-risk stratum. In the offer arm, follow-up is observed for 72 of 80 lower-risk people, with 36 successes, and 20 of 40 higher-risk people, with 12 successes. The stratum-specific rates are therefore 36/72 = 50% and 12/20 = 60%; applying the assigned shares gives (2/3)(0.50) + (1/3)(0.60) = 53.3%. In the comparison arm, the corresponding observed counts are 64 of 80 with 24 successes and 36 of 40 with 18 successes, giving 37.5% and 50%, so standardization gives (2/3)(0.375) + (1/3)(0.50) = 41.7%. The standardized difference is 11.7 percentage points, versus 48/92 − 42/100 = 10.2 points using unweighted complete cases. This adjustment is defensible only if, within treatment and baseline stratum, follow-up is unrelated to the missing outcome (a MAR-style assumption); inspect whether the strata are sufficiently predictive and report sensitivity if that assumption is doubtful.
selection-missing-data.Conditioning on who is observed can chan: A useful sensitivity check is to bound an outcome rather than silently fill in missing cases. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the outcome is a 0–10 training-test score, with 18% of the offer group and 12% of the comparison group missing. Among observed cases, the means are 7.2 and 5.8, so the observed-case gap is 7.2 − 5.8 = 1.4 score points. Keep the assigned denominators: the offer-group overall mean is 0.82(7.2) + 0.18mₒ = 5.904 + 0.18mₒ, while the comparison mean is 0.88(5.8) + 0.12m𝚌 = 5.104 + 0.12m𝚌, where mₒ and m𝚌 are unknown missing-case means. Using only the known 0–10 range, the smallest gap sets mₒ = 0 and m𝚌 = 10: 5.904 − 6.304 = −0.400 points. The largest sets mₒ = 10 and m𝚌 = 0: 7.704 − 5.104 = 2.600 points. Thus the data alone permit a −0.4 to 2.6 point range, not a precise effect. If assignment was randomized, this can be an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis; otherwise it is descriptive, not causal. The lab’s attrition and unseen-outcome controls illustrate the same logic, but their values are teaching assumptions, not observed data.

heterogeneous-effects.An average can hide variation: Suppose a randomized childcare-subsidy offer is evaluated with baseline care access defined in advance. In a synthetic example, parents with high access have participation of 62% without the offer and 68% with it, so their subgroup average effect is 68 − 62 = 6 percentage points. Parents with low access move from 41% to 53%, giving 12 percentage points. The interaction contrast asks whether those effects differ: (53 − 41) − (68 − 62) = 12 − 6 = 6 percentage points, not whether one subgroup’s separate test is significant and the other is not. If 40% of the target population has high access and 60% low access, the corresponding standardized average is 0.40×6 + 0.60×12 = 9.6 percentage points; changing those population shares changes the overall estimand, not the subgroup effects. These figures are illustrative and synthetic, not observed outcomes. For a causal interpretation, random assignment must be credible within the pre-specified groups, participation must be measured on the same follow-up window, and uncertainty for the 6-point interaction should be reported directly. This interaction is a probability-scale contrast; a quantile-regression coefficient would answer a different distributional question.
heterogeneous-effects.Read interaction terms carefully: Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): suppose a logistic model predicts whether a household takes a training course, with treatment T and a pre-treatment income indicator H (1 for high income). Let the fitted logit be logit[P(Y=1)] = −1.20 + 0.50T + 0.80H − 0.30(T×H). First compute the treated-minus-untreated contrast separately on the probability scale. For H=0, the untreated probability is logistic(−1.20)=0.231 and the treated probability is logistic(−0.70)=0.332, so the predicted contrast is 0.101, or 10.1 percentage points. For H=1, the corresponding linear predictors are −0.40 and −0.10; logistic(−0.40)=0.401 and logistic(−0.10)=0.475, giving 7.4 percentage points. The difference in predicted treatment contrasts is therefore 7.4−10.1 = −2.7 percentage points—not −0.30, because the interaction coefficient is on the log-odds scale. Treat these as model-based average predictions, not individual effects; report uncertainty for the direct contrast of contrasts, and check that probabilities remain plausible over the observed income range. A causal interpretation still requires treatment assignment or other identification assumptions.
heterogeneous-effects.Quantile regression answers a distributi: A useful follow-up to the displayed subgroup estimates is to test a contrast directly. Take a synthetic lab setting with total sample size n = 120, average effect 0.8 outcome units, and subgroup spread 0.6 units. The implied subgroup estimates are A = 0.8 − 0.6 = 0.2, B = 0.8, and C = 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.4 units. Using the lab’s illustrative standard error, SE = 1.4/√(120/3) = 0.221 units, each 95% reference interval has half-width 1.96 × 0.221 = 0.434 units. The scientifically targeted comparison is C − A = 1.4 − 0.2 = 1.2 units, not whether C’s interval excludes zero while A’s does not. If the two subgroup estimates were independent with this same SE, SE(C − A) = √(0.221² + 0.221²) = 0.313 units, giving z = 1.2/0.313 = 3.83 and an approximate 95% interval of 1.2 ± 1.96(0.313) = [0.586, 1.814] units. In real data, covariance, unequal sizes, and pre-specified subgroup definitions change this calculation; even a precise contrast is not causal without identification assumptions.
heterogeneous-effects.Keep discovery and confirmation distinct: Suppose, purely illustratively, a pre-specified childcare-subsidy analysis estimates a participation increase of 2.0 percentage points for parents with reliable backup care (standard error 0.8 points) and 5.0 percentage points for those without it (standard error 1.0 point). The heterogeneity estimand is the difference in subgroup effects, 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 percentage points—not a comparison of which subgroup has a smaller p-value. If the two subgroup estimates come from disjoint samples and their errors are independent, the standard error of that contrast is √(0.8² + 1.0²) = √1.64 ≈ 1.28 percentage points. A normal-approximation 95% interval is therefore 3.0 ± 1.96 × 1.28, or approximately 0.49 to 5.51 percentage points. This interval describes uncertainty about the difference in average effects, not an effect for a particular parent. Independence is an assumption: with overlapping observations or shared fitted parameters, use the covariance-adjusted variance Var(τ̂₂ − τ̂₁) = Var(τ̂₂) + Var(τ̂₁) − 2Cov(τ̂₂,τ̂₁). Even a positive contrast remains conditional on credible treatment assignment, outcome measurement and pre-specified group definitions.
heterogeneous-effects.Conditional quantiles are not individual: Consider a pre-specified interaction for the childcare example. Suppose, purely illustratively, a randomized subsidy study estimates a monthly participation-related earnings effect of 120 currency units for parents with high baseline care access and 40 currency units for parents with low access. Code high access as G = 1 and low access as G = 0; in a linear outcome model, the interaction coefficient is the conditional contrast 120 − 40 = 80 currency units per month. If the two subgroup estimates have standard errors of 30 and 25 currency units and their estimation errors are treated as uncorrelated for this illustration, the contrast standard error is √(30² + 25²) = √1,525 ≈ 39.1 currency units per month. A normal-approximation 95% interval is therefore 80 ± 1.96(39.1), or about 3.4 to 156.6 currency units per month. This supports a positive difference under the stated approximation, but it is not an individual treatment effect or a quantile coefficient. The grouping variable must be measured before treatment; random assignment (or a defensible conditional-exchangeability design) is needed for causal interpretation, and unequal variances or correlated estimates require the appropriate covariance-aware standard error.
heterogeneous-effects.Test the difference between groups direc: Consider a synthetic childcare-subsidy example in which the outcome is labour-force participation, measured as a probability. Pre-specify baseline care access as the subgroup indicator, then compare treated and untreated parents within each group. If participation is 35% without and 47% with the subsidy among low-access parents, their estimated effect is 47% − 35% = 12 percentage points. Suppose the corresponding high-access figures are 62% and 68%, giving 6 percentage points. The interaction contrast is therefore 12 − 6 = 6 percentage points: the estimated subsidy effect is larger for the low-access group by six percentage points, not “six percent.” If 40% of the target population is low-access and 60% high-access, the standardized average effect would be 0.40×12 + 0.60×6 = 4.8 + 3.6 = 8.4 percentage points, so subgroup effects need not equal the overall effect. These numbers are illustrative, synthetic values, not observed data. The interpretation requires credible treatment comparisons within both pre-treatment groups, a common outcome definition and adequate sample support; calculate uncertainty for the six-point interaction before making a policy claim.

functional-form-specification.Keep units attached to every coefficient: A quadratic term makes the coefficient on the level term only part of the calculation. Consider this explicitly synthetic model for monthly pay, measured in dollars, where x is years of training: predicted pay = 2,400 + 300x − 20x². The 300 has units of dollars per month per training year, while −20 has units of dollars per month per training-year squared. To compare 8 with 9 years, calculate the change directly: 300(9−8) − 20(9²−8²) = 300 − 20(17) = −40 dollars per month. Indeed, the predictions are 3,520 dollars at x = 8 and 3,480 dollars at x = 9. The local marginal effect is 300 − 40x, so it is −20 dollars per month per additional year at x = 8; the fitted maximum occurs where this equals zero, x = 7.5 years. Thus, do not read 300 as the effect at every training level. This interpretation is descriptive of the fitted curve, not evidence that training causes pay, and the turning point is especially fragile if the data contain few observations near it or the model is extrapolated beyond the observed range.
functional-form-specification.Allow curvature when the question calls: Suppose, purely illustratively, that a synthetic wage model measures hourly pay in dollars and experience x in years: W(x) = 20 + 1.2x − 0.1x². The slope is not 1.2 dollars everywhere; differentiating gives dW/dx = 1.2 − 0.2x dollars per additional year. Thus the model predicts a gain of 0.4 dollars per hour at 4 years, zero marginal change at x = 6, and a decline of 0.4 dollars per hour at 8 years. The turning point is −1.2/[2(−0.1)] = 6 years, where predicted pay is 20 + 7.2 − 3.6 = 23.6 dollars per hour. A discrete check from 5 to 6 years gives W(5) = 23.5 and W(6) = 23.6, an increase of 0.1 dollar per hour; from 6 to 7, W(7) = 23.5, a decrease of 0.1. This is a model-implied association, not a causal return to schooling or experience: omitted ability, cohort differences, and sparse observations near 8 years could change the curve. In the specification lab, compare the quadratic’s lower in-sample error with residual patterns and held-out performance before trusting the turning point.
functional-form-specification.Interactions compare conditional slopes: Consider a synthetic demand model where weekly sales q are measured in units, discount d in percentage points, and household income i in thousands of pounds: q = 120 + 4d − 1.5i + 0.2(di). The marginal association of discount is the derivative ∂q/∂d = 4 + 0.2i units per percentage point. At i = 20, one additional percentage point of discount corresponds to 8 more units per week; at i = 35, it corresponds to 11 more, so the conditional-slope difference is 3 units per percentage point, computed as 0.2 × (35 − 20). For a transparent intercept, center income at £20,000: with i_c = i − 20, the same equation is q = 90 + 8d − 1.5i_c + 0.2(di_c). Now the coefficient 8 describes the discount slope at the meaningful reference income, rather than at zero income. These are explicitly illustrative synthetic values, not observed demand. Check that discounts and incomes lie within the sample’s support; otherwise the slope comparison is extrapolation. The interaction is an association unless a credible design supports a causal pricing claim, and residual or nonlinear-fit checks can reveal misspecification.
functional-form-specification.Check specification without chasing a pr: Use held-out prediction to test whether an apparently useful curve travels beyond the observations that shaped it. For an illustrative synthetic dataset of 30 apartments, split the rows into five folds of six, fit each specification on the other 24 rows, and predict the six held-out rents; keep the folds identical for both models. Suppose the five held-out sums of squared errors (SSE), in dollars squared, are 18, 20, 16, 22, and 19 for the linear model, versus 16, 19, 18, 20, and 17 for the quadratic model. The totals are 95 and 90 dollars squared, so the cross-validated RMSEs are √(95/30) = $1.78 and √(90/30) = $1.73 per apartment-month, respectively. The quadratic model therefore improves held-out RMSE by about $0.05, or roughly 2.7% relative to $1.78, in this synthetic illustration. Because the gain is small and fold-specific errors differ, inspect prediction intervals and sensitivity to the fold assignment before preferring the curve. This checks predictive stability, not causal validity; it also cannot justify extrapolating beyond the observed commute-distance range.
functional-form-specification.Trace omitted-variable bias through two: A useful diagnostic is to translate the bias into the same units as the reported coefficient. Consider an explicitly synthetic evaluation of a remote-work subsidy: after controlling for observed age and occupation, the earnings gap is +$180 per month, but commute reliability, U, remains omitted. Among comparable workers, subsidy recipients average 0.5 standard deviations higher on U, while a separate conditional outcome relationship assigns U a slope of −$200 per month per standard deviation. The implied omitted-variable component is (0.5 SD) × (−$200/month/SD) = −$100 per month. Because the observed gap equals the target effect plus this component in the additive linear approximation, a bias-corrected descriptive estimate would be +$180 − (−$100) = +$280 per month, not +$80. This arithmetic is illustrative, not an observed estimate: it assumes the U gap and outcome slope refer to the same conditioning set, uses a correctly measured pre-treatment U, and ignores nonlinearities and interactions. A residual plot or a better-fitting curve in the specification lab cannot verify those confounding assumptions; it can only flag model-form problems in the simulated outcome relationship.

applied-macro-time-series.Inspect time order and measurement first: To make a forecast check reproducible, use a rolling origin and freeze the information set at each origin. For an explicitly illustrative synthetic quarterly unemployment rate, suppose the long-run level is 5.0%, the latest vintage reports 6.2%, and a centered AR(1) persistence parameter is φ = 0.75. The one-quarter-ahead forecast is 5.0% + 0.75(6.2% − 5.0%) = 5.9%; the two-quarter forecast is 5.0% + 0.75²(1.2 percentage points) = 5.675%. If the innovation standard deviation is assumed to be 0.4 percentage points, the forecast standard deviations are 0.4 percentage points at one quarter and 0.4√(1 + 0.75²) ≈ 0.50 percentage points at two quarters. A rough normal 95% interval for the second forecast is therefore 5.675% ± 1.96(0.50 percentage points), or about 4.70% to 6.65%. At the next quarter, compare that stored forecast with the newly available observation, then move the origin forward and repeat; do not refit using later revisions when evaluating an earlier forecast. This tests predictive accuracy, not whether persistence caused unemployment or whether the assumed AR(1) form is structurally stable.
applied-macro-time-series.Separate trend from persistence: To separate persistence from a level forecast, center the series on a reference mean and model the deviation y_t. Suppose, illustratively with synthetic monthly data, an inflation deviation is y_t = 1.5 percentage points, the AR(1) persistence parameter is φ = 0.80, and the innovation standard deviation is σ = 0.60 percentage points per month. The one-, two-, and three-month conditional mean deviations are 0.80(1.5) = 1.20, 0.80²(1.5) = 0.96, and 0.80³(1.5) = 0.768 percentage points: the shock fades toward zero rather than being added repeatedly. Forecast uncertainty can be built recursively: V₁ = 0.60² = 0.36, V₂ = 0.36 + 0.80²(0.36) = 0.5904, and V₃ = 0.36 + 0.80²(0.5904) = 0.737856, so the standard deviations are 0.60, 0.768, and about 0.859 percentage points. A 95% half-width is 1.96 times each SD, or 1.176, 1.506, and 1.684 percentage points. This interpretation assumes a stable |φ| < 1 process and mean-zero innovations; changing policy regimes or seasonal structure can invalidate it, and forecasting does not identify what caused the initial shock.
applied-macro-time-series.Build forecasts using only past informat: Suppose, purely illustratively, that a monthly unemployment-rate deviation from its long-run mean is +1.2 percentage points at the forecast origin. A zero-mean AR(1) model with persistence φ = 0.75 and innovation standard deviation σ = 0.4 percentage points gives the one-month-ahead mean as 0.75 × 1.2 = 0.90 percentage points, and the two-month-ahead mean as 0.75² × 1.2 = 0.675 percentage points. Uncertainty accumulates new shocks: at horizon 1, variance = 0.4² = 0.16 (percentage points)², so SD = 0.40 percentage points; at horizon 2, variance = 0.16 + 0.75² × 0.16 = 0.25 (percentage points)², so SD = 0.50 percentage points. A rough 95% interval is 0.90 ± 1.96(0.40) = 0.116 to 1.684 percentage points at one month, and 0.675 ± 1.96(0.50) = −0.305 to 1.655 percentage points at two months. These are forecasts of a deviation, not levels or a causal effect. They rely on stable persistence, constant innovation variance, and a zero long-run mean—assumptions to check, not silently import.
applied-macro-time-series.Dynamic responses are model-dependent: To see why the forecast band widens, use an illustrative synthetic AR(1) model, Y_t = 0.8Y_{t−1} + ε_t, with innovation standard deviation σ = 0.6 series units and a final observed value of Y_T = 2 units. The three conditional forecast means are 0.8(2) = 1.6 units, 0.8²(2) = 1.28 units, and 0.8³(2) = 1.024 units: persistence moves the mean toward the model’s zero level, rather than adding 2 units at every date. Forecast variance must also accumulate: at horizon 3 it is σ²[1 + 0.8² + 0.8⁴] = 0.36(1 + 0.64 + 0.4096) = 0.737856 units², so the standard deviation is about 0.859 units. A normal-reference 95% band around the third-step mean is therefore 1.024 ± 1.96(0.859), or approximately −0.660 to 2.708 units. These are conditional model summaries, not observed outcomes; the interval relies on the innovation and stability assumptions, and neither persistence nor a good forecast identifies a causal policy shock. A structural break could make both the decay and the band misleading.
applied-macro-time-series.An AR(1) forecast mean-reverts toward it: An additional diagnostic is the persistence half-life: the number of periods needed for the model’s forecast mean to shrink to half its current deviation. For an illustrative synthetic AR(1) with φ = 0.80 and a final observed deviation of −2.5 percentage points from the long-run mean, solve 0.80^h = 0.5: h = ln(0.5) / ln(0.80) ≈ 3.11 periods. The six-period forecast is not halfway again by an informal rule; it is (0.80)^6(−2.5) = 0.262144(−2.5) = −0.65536 percentage points, so the expected deviation retains about 26.2% of its initial magnitude. A negative starting deviation remains negative in the conditional mean because φ is positive, while each future innovation can move the realized series above or below that path. In the interactive lab, changing persistence changes both this decay rate and the uncertainty accumulation, whereas changing the horizon simply asks how far along the same model path to look. The half-life describes model-implied persistence, not a causal effect of a policy or a guaranteed date of recovery; a break or changing measurement definition would invalidate the calculation.
applied-macro-time-series.Serial dependence means monthly rows are: Use the forecast origin to separate persistence from new uncertainty. For an illustrative synthetic AR(1) series with zero long-run mean, suppose the last observed value is 2.00 units, persistence is φ = 0.65, the innovation standard deviation is 0.60 units per period, and the horizon is three periods. The one-step, two-step and three-step forecast means are respectively 0.65(2.00) = 1.30, 0.65²(2.00) = 0.845, and 0.65³(2.00) = 0.549 units: the old deviation decays rather than being added repeatedly. The three-step forecast-error variance is 0.60²[1 + 0.65² + 0.65⁴] = 0.576 units², so its standard deviation is √0.576 = 0.759 units. A normal-reference 95% band is therefore 0.549 ± 1.96(0.759), or approximately −0.939 to 2.037 units. The band is a conditional forecast interval, not a confidence interval for a causal policy effect. It also depends on stationarity, a stable φ, correctly specified innovation variance, and no intervening structural break; re-estimation and forecast evaluation should use only information available at each date.

multilevel-partial-pooling.Why a group label can matter: Suppose, purely illustratively, that eight synthetic observations from Office A imply a mean placement rate of 68 percentage points, while the four-office grand mean is 60 percentage points. Use the lab’s known-variance normal-normal illustration with within-office standard deviation σ = 4 percentage points and between-office standard deviation τ = 2 percentage points. First compute the local-mean precision, n/σ² = 8/16 = 0.5, and the prior (between-office) precision, 1/τ² = 1/4 = 0.25. The weight on Office A’s local estimate is therefore λ = 0.5/(0.5 + 0.25) = 2/3. The partially pooled estimate is 60 + (2/3)(68 − 60) = 60 + 5.33 = 65.33 percentage points, rather than either 68 or 60. Thus the model treats the office as above the overall level while tempering a noisy small-sample contrast. If n rose, λ would increase; if σ rose, it would decrease. This is estimation of a modeled office difference, not evidence that the office caused placement outcomes, and the calculation assumes comparable group sizes and correctly specified variance components; unequal sizes require group-specific weights.
multilevel-partial-pooling.The two extremes: pool everything or not: Consider an illustrative synthetic wage-outcome example with four regions, each having n = 9 workers. Suppose the within-region standard deviation is σ = 3 outcome units and the between-region standard deviation is τ = 1.5 outcome units; treat both variance components as known, as in the teaching lab. If the synthetic regional mean is 56 and the synthetic grand mean is 50, the partial-pooling weight on the local mean is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 1.5²/(1.5² + 3²/9) = 2.25/(2.25 + 1) = 0.692. The pooled estimate is therefore 50 + 0.692(56 − 50) = 54.15 outcome units: it moves 1.85 units toward the common mean, rather than declaring 56 to be a precise regional level. A region with mean 47 would instead receive 50 + 0.692(47 − 50) = 47.92. Increasing n raises λ because σ²/n falls, so the data receive more weight; increasing τ also raises λ because genuine regional differences are modeled as larger. This is descriptive shrinkage, not evidence that region caused wages, and unequal group sizes require group-specific weights.
multilevel-partial-pooling.Partial pooling tempers noisy group esti: A useful diagnostic is to recompute the same group mean under two sample sizes while holding the observed mean fixed. Use an illustrative synthetic outcome measured in monthly percentage points: a group mean is 4.2 pp, the observed grand mean is 2.0 pp, the within-group SD is σ = 3 pp, and the between-group SD is τ = 1.5 pp. With n = 9, the known-variance teaching weight is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 2.25/(2.25 + 9/9) = 2.25/3.25 ≈ 0.692. The partially pooled estimate is 2.0 + 0.692(4.2 − 2.0) = 2.0 + 1.522 ≈ 3.52 pp. If a later, equally precise-looking group mean of 4.2 pp came from n = 36 instead, λ = 2.25/(2.25 + 9/36) = 2.25/2.50 = 0.90, so the estimate becomes 2.0 + 0.90(2.2) = 3.98 pp. Thus the same gap receives different borrowing because σ²/n changes. This is a sensitivity calculation, not evidence that the larger group is causally better: unequal variances, missing outcomes, or estimated τ can alter the weight.
multilevel-partial-pooling.Read a varying-intercept model: To see the mechanics of shrinkage, consider an explicitly synthetic example of four employment offices with equal samples. Suppose the overall mean placement rate is 50%, Office A’s unpooled sample mean is 62%, the within-office standard deviation is σ = 10 percentage points, the between-office standard deviation is τ = 4 percentage points, and n = 16 people are observed in each office. Under the lab’s known-variance normal-normal illustration, the weight on Office A’s local signal is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 16/(16 + 100/16) = 16/22.25 ≈ 0.719. The partially pooled estimate is therefore 50% + 0.719(62% − 50%) = 50% + 8.63 percentage points = 58.63%. It remains above the overall mean, but moves 3.37 percentage points toward it because 16 observations leave sampling noise. Increasing n would reduce σ²/n and raise λ; increasing within-office variation would lower λ. This calculation assumes comparable office sizes, a suitable model, and known variance components; in fitted data, estimating τ and σ adds uncertainty, and the result is not proof that Office A causes better placement.
multilevel-partial-pooling.Know what the design can support: Consider an explicitly illustrative synthetic wage index with four offices, known within-office SD σ = 2 wage-index units, and assumed between-office SD τ = 1.5 units. Suppose the observed grand mean is 10, and Office A’s mean is 12 from n = 16 workers. Its sampling variance is σ²/n = 4/16 = 0.25, so the normal-normal partial-pooling weight on A’s deviation is λ = τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) = 2.25/(2.25 + 0.25) = 0.90. The pooled estimate is therefore 10 + 0.90(12 − 10) = 11.8 wage-index units: it moves 0.2 units toward the grand mean, rather than declaring the local mean exact. If the same mean came from n = 4, λ would be 2.25/(2.25 + 1) = 0.692, giving 11.38 units, because the local estimate is noisier. These calculations describe modeled office differences, not productivity effects or causes. In the actual lab, σ and τ are teaching inputs and group sizes are equal; with unequal sizes or estimated variance components, uncertainty in those inputs must also be reported.

complex-survey-sampling.Start with the population, frame and sel: Consider an illustrative, synthetic labour-market survey of 1,000 firms whose frame covers 600 micro firms and 400 larger firms. Suppose the design selects 60 micro firms (selection probability 0.10) and 80 larger firms (probability 0.20), and the corresponding respondent mean monthly wage is 19 currency units for micro firms and 36 currency units for larger firms. The unweighted respondent mean is (60×19 + 80×36)/140 = 28.71 currency units, but it overrepresents the larger stratum. An inverse-probability estimate of the population total is 60×19/0.10 + 80×36/0.20 = 11,400 + 14,400 = 25,800 currency units across the 1,000 firms; dividing by the known population size gives an estimated mean of 25.80 currency units per firm. Equivalently, the stratum shares are 0.60 and 0.40, so the benchmark calculation is 0.60×19 + 0.40×36 = 25.80. This interpretation requires complete frame coverage, known non-zero selection probabilities, and roughly random selection within each stratum; weighting does not repair nonresponse or biased within-stratum wage reporting.
complex-survey-sampling.Weights reflect unequal chances of selec: Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): suppose a labour-force survey samples three strata and records estimated unemployment rates of 4% in stratum A, 8% in B and 15% in C. The sample contains 50, 60 and 40 people, while the target population counts are 5,000, 3,000 and 2,000. Start by checking each base weight: 5,000/50 = 100 for A, 3,000/60 = 50 for B, and 2,000/40 = 50 for C. Treating the within-stratum rates as sample estimates, the estimated unemployed count is 100(50)(0.04) + 50(60)(0.08) + 50(40)(0.15) = 200 + 240 + 300 = 740 people. The weighted population denominator is 5,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = 10,000, so the estimated unemployment rate is 740/10,000 = 0.074, or 7.4%. An equal-weight average of the three stratum rates would be (4% + 8% + 15%)/3 = 9.0%, which answers a different question because it gives each stratum equal influence rather than each person. Before reporting 7.4%, verify that the population counts and non-zero selection probabilities are appropriate; differential nonresponse or misclassified strata can still bias every weighted component.
complex-survey-sampling.Strata and clusters solve different fiel: Suppose, purely illustratively, that annual household food spending averages $24,000 in an urban stratum and $12,000 in a rural stratum. If those strata comprise 75% and 25% of the target population, the population-weighted estimate is 0.75 × $24,000 + 0.25 × $12,000 = $21,000 per household-year. A sample containing 60% urban and 40% rural households would instead have the raw mean 0.60 × $24,000 + 0.40 × $12,000 = $19,200, a $1,800 understatement caused by composition. The corresponding calibration factors are 0.75/0.60 = 1.25 for urban respondents and 0.25/0.40 = 0.625 for rural respondents; applying them and dividing by their weighted share total reproduces $21,000. This fixes unequal representation only under the illustrative assumption that each stratum mean is adequately measured; it does not prove nonresponse is ignorable. For uncertainty, suppose 120 respondents came as 8 equal-size neighbourhood clusters of 15 and an illustrative within-cluster correlation was ρ = 0.15. The rough design effect 1 + (15 − 1)ρ = 3.10 gives an effective-size diagnostic of 120/3.10 ≈ 38.7, not 120 independent observations.
complex-survey-sampling.Let the sample design govern uncertainty: A useful check is to separate stratified sampling variance from the point-estimate calculation. Suppose, purely illustratively, that the target population is 30% stratum A and 70% stratum B, and the outcome is weekly earnings in currency units. If independent within-stratum samples give n_A = 50 with s_A = 12 currency units and n_B = 100 with s_B = 20, the estimated population mean is μ̂ = 0.30ȳ_A + 0.70ȳ_B, while an approximate variance (before finite-population corrections) is (0.30² × 12²/50) + (0.70² × 20²/100) = 0.2592 + 1.9600 = 2.2192 currency-units². Thus SE(μ̂) = √2.2192 ≈ 1.49 currency units, and a normal-reference 95% margin is 1.96 × 1.49 ≈ 2.92 currency units. The squared weights matter: the larger, more variable stratum contributes most of the uncertainty. This calculation assumes independent observations within each stratum and correctly defined stratum shares; if the sample also selects clusters, a PSU-aware variance method must replace this shortcut, and nonresponse adjustment requires its own justification.
complex-survey-sampling.Treat nonresponse as a separate stage: A useful diagnostic is to separate the weighted respondent estimate from a plausible nonresponse sensitivity range. Suppose, purely illustratively, that a synthetic labour survey targets 70% urban and 30% rural workers, and the respondent means are 35 and 25 hours per week. If the adjustment cells are those two groups, the benchmark-weighted respondent estimate is 0.70×35 + 0.30×25 = 32 hours per week. This is not yet a guarantee: imagine rural nonrespondents would average 31 hours, while rural respondents average 25, with a 50% rural response rate; the implied rural all-selected mean is (0.50×25) + (0.50×31) = 28 hours, so the corresponding population mean becomes 0.70×35 + 0.30×28 = 32.9 hours per week, 0.9 hours above the respondent-based estimate. Urban nonrespondents were assumed equal to urban respondents in this illustration, not observed to be so. Report that assumption and vary it in sensitivity analysis. Finally, do not confuse this bias check with precision: under the lab’s equal-cluster approximation, m = 20 and ρ = 0.20 give DEFF = 1 + 19×0.20 = 4.8, so 600 records represent roughly 600/4.8 = 125 independent observations for variance intuition.

survival-duration-analysis.Duration outcomes contain time and statu: To see how status and follow-up enter a Kaplan–Meier estimate, use this illustrative synthetic cohort of eight claimants. Suppose re-employment is observed at months 2, 5, 5, and 9; other spells are censored at months 4, 7, 10, and 12. Start with eight people at risk. At month 2, one event gives S(2) = (8−1)/8 = 7/8 = 0.875. The month-4 censoring is removed before the next event time, so six people remain at risk at month 5; two events give S(5) = 0.875 × (6−2)/6 = 0.5833. The month-7 censoring then leaves three at risk at month 9; one event gives S(9) = 0.5833 × (3−1)/3 = 0.3889, or 38.9% estimated event-free. Thus the estimated median duration is 9 months, the first event time at which survival is at most 0.5—not the average observed spell. Censoring at months 10 and 12 does not change S(9). This calculation assumes censoring is unrelated to imminent re-employment, at least conditional on relevant observed information; administrative closure may be plausible, but selective loss from the data system can violate that assumption.
survival-duration-analysis.Right-censoring is partial information,: Here is a synthetic illustration of why a hazard ratio must be translated through time before discussing risk. Suppose a constant monthly event hazard is λ = 0.04, and follow-up lasts 12 months. The event-free probability is S(12) = exp(−0.04 × 12) = exp(−0.48) ≈ 0.619, so the model-implied probability of an event by 12 months is 1 − 0.619 = 0.381, or 38.1%. If a comparison group has hazard ratio 1.5, its hazard is 0.04 × 1.5 = 0.06 per month; its corresponding survival is exp(−0.06 × 12) = exp(−0.72) ≈ 0.487, implying 51.3% experiencing the event and an illustrative absolute difference of 13.2 percentage points. These are synthetic model calculations, not observed outcomes, and the absolute gap depends on the time horizon and baseline hazard. The calculation also assumes a constant hazard and correctly specified comparison; censoring does not turn the 38.1% or 51.3% into observed proportions unless follow-up and censoring assumptions support that interpretation. A changing hazard would require integrating λ(t), rather than multiplying one rate by time.
survival-duration-analysis.Read the survival curve and median: Use the lab’s smooth curves as a model-to-probability calculation, not as a replacement for the Kaplan–Meier risk table. Suppose, purely illustratively, that a baseline monthly hazard is λ = 0.04 and a comparison group has hazard ratio HR = 1.50. Under the constant-hazard assumption, the comparison hazard is 0.04 × 1.50 = 0.06 per month. At t = 6 months, baseline survival is S₀(6) = exp(−0.04 × 6) = exp(−0.24) ≈ 0.787, so the modeled event probability by six months is 1 − 0.787 = 0.213, or 21.3%. Comparison survival is S₁(6) = exp(−0.06 × 6) = exp(−0.36) ≈ 0.698, giving 30.2% by six months. The hazard ratio is 1.50, but the six-month event-probability ratio is 0.302/0.213 ≈ 1.42, not 1.50; translating hazards requires the time horizon and baseline hazard. Treat these values as synthetic illustrations: real hazards may vary with time, and censoring assumptions and model fit must be checked before interpreting a group contrast.
survival-duration-analysis.Hazard is conditional on still being at: For a concrete synthetic illustration, suppose an unemployment spell has a constant re-employment hazard of 0.04 per month in a baseline group, and a comparison programme is assigned a hazard ratio of 0.75. First multiply the rate: 0.04 × 0.75 = 0.03 per month. Over 12 months, the cumulative hazards are 0.04 × 12 = 0.48 and 0.03 × 12 = 0.36, so the model-implied survival probabilities are S₀(12) = exp(−0.48) ≈ 0.619 and S₁(12) = exp(−0.36) ≈ 0.698. Thus the corresponding event probabilities are about 38.1% and 30.2%, a difference of roughly 7.9 percentage points; the hazard ratio itself is not 7.9% and cannot be converted to that difference without the baseline hazard and time horizon. This calculation assumes a constant hazard and proportional hazards, with no informative censoring after conditioning on the model’s covariates. In the lab, changing the censoring slider should not move these curves: it represents incomplete observation, not extra re-employment. If censoring is related to unobserved re-employment prospects, the displayed survival interpretation may be biased.
survival-duration-analysis.Check whether the comparison remains cre: Use the lab’s constant-hazard model to translate a relative hazard into an absolute 12-month comparison. Suppose the illustrative baseline monthly hazard is λ = 0.05 and the comparison hazard ratio is HR = 0.75, so the comparison hazard is 0.05 × 0.75 = 0.0375 per month. Under a constant-hazard and independent-censoring assumption, baseline survival at 12 months is S₀(12) = exp(−0.05 × 12) = exp(−0.60) ≈ 0.5488, while comparison survival is S₁(12) = exp(−0.0375 × 12) = exp(−0.45) ≈ 0.6376. Thus the modeled event risks by month 12 are 1 − S₀ = 45.1% and 1 − S₁ = 36.2%, an absolute difference of about 8.9 percentage points in this synthetic illustration. The HR of 0.75 describes a 25% lower instantaneous hazard (1 − 0.75), not a 25-percentage-point reduction in 12-month event probability. If censoring is related to impending re-employment even after conditioning on modeled information, these curve calculations need sensitivity analysis; censoring is not an event.

spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.A map is data with a geography: To see why the weights rule is part of the estimand, use an explicitly synthetic four-region example with outcomes measured in percentage points: A = 2, B = 4, C = 8, and D = 10. Suppose C’s rook neighbors are B and D, each with weight 1. Its row-standardized spatial lag is (1×4 + 1×10)/(1+1) = 7 percentage points, meaning the average outcome assigned to C by this rule is 7 pp. Now add diagonal region A with weight 0.5 while retaining B and D at weight 1. The lag becomes (1×4 + 1×10 + 0.5×2)/(1+1+0.5) = 15/2.5 = 6 pp. The one-unit change is produced by the neighbourhood definition, not by new observations or a change in C. If these outcomes are rates, this equal-region average also implicitly gives a tiny and populous region the same influence; population-weighted or distance-based weights would answer a different question. A high lag or positive Moran’s I still describes patterned similarity, not evidence that neighbours caused C’s outcome; causal spillovers require a defensible design and assumptions.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Neighbourhoods become a weights matrix: Suppose an analyst uses a distance-informed rule for a synthetic, illustrative rental-inflation index measured in percentage points. For focal district C, four edge-sharing neighbours have values 6, 8, 10, and 12 pp, while four corner neighbours have values 4, 16, 9, and 11 pp; assign raw weight 1 to edge links and 0.3 to corner links. The weighted numerator is (6+8+10+12) + 0.3(4+16+9+11) = 36 + 12 = 48 pp-weight units, and the row total is 4 + 0.3×4 = 5.2 weight units. C’s row-standardized lag is therefore 48/5.2 = 9.23 pp, not the unweighted eight-neighbour average, 76/8 = 9.50 pp. The denominator matters because boundary districts may have fewer links, and changing the diagonal slider changes both numerator and denominator. In the interactive lab, the same normalization idea is applied to standardized synthetic outcomes on a 6×6 grid before the Moran scatter is drawn; its Moran’s I is descriptive for that generated field and has no permutation p-value. Neither lag, nor a high Moran’s I, identifies a spillover without a defensible causal design.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Moran’s I summarizes global similarity a: A useful diagnostic before interpreting a global index is to compute one local point exactly. Consider an illustrative synthetic focal district with standardized unemployment value zᵢ = 1.5. Suppose its four rook neighbours have z values 1.0, 0.6, 0.2 and 0.8, while its four diagonal neighbours have −0.4, 0.0, 0.2 and 0.4. If rook links have weight 1 and diagonal links have weight 0.5, the row sum is 4 + 4(0.5) = 6. The weighted neighbour total is 2.6 + 0.5(0.2) = 2.7, so the row-normalized spatial lag is 2.7/6 = 0.45. The corresponding Moran-scatter product for this district is zᵢ × lagᵢ = 1.5 × 0.45 = 0.675, a high–high contribution, but it is not a standalone local significance test. If diagonal weight were set to zero, the lag would instead be 2.6/4 = 0.65; the apparent local association changes because the neighbourhood definition changed, not because unemployment data changed. Standardization also means 1.5 and 0.45 are SD units, not percentage points. This is why compare settings and inspect the map before attributing a regional pattern to spillovers.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Spatial lag and spatial error tell diffe: To see how a global association is assembled, use this illustrative four-region line, not observed data. Suppose standardized rental-growth values are z = (−1, −0.5, 0.5, 1), and each interior region averages its two adjacent neighbours while an endpoint uses its one neighbour. The resulting spatial lags are (−0.5, −0.25, 0.25, 0.5). Using the same row-normalized convention as the lab, the numerator is Σzᵢ(Wz)ᵢ = (−1)(−0.5) + (−0.5)(−0.25) + (0.5)(0.25) + (1)(0.5) = 1.25. The denominator is Σzᵢ² = 1 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 1 = 2.5, so the Moran-style ratio is 1.25/2.5 = 0.50. That positive value says high and low standardized outcomes tend to sit beside similar values under this chosen neighbour rule; it does not say a rail investment transmitted rental inflation. In the site’s 6×6 synthetic grid, changing ρ, diagonal weight, or the local shock changes the computed statistic. A randomization reference would additionally ask whether 0.40 is unusual after shuffling values across fixed locations; without that comparison, the number is descriptive, and edge handling and weights remain substantive assumptions.
spatial-dependence-regional-econometrics.Stress-test the geography and causal cla: To move from a global signal to a local diagnostic, work cell by cell rather than calling every high Moran’s I result a cluster. In an illustrative synthetic 6×6 grid, suppose one region has standardized rent-growth residual zᵢ = 1.5 and its four equal-weight rook neighbours have z = 1.0, 0.8, −0.2, and 0.4. Its spatial lag is the weighted mean, (1.0 + 0.8 − 0.2 + 0.4) / 4 = 0.50, so the local cross-product zᵢ × lagᵢ = 1.5 × 0.50 = 0.75: a high value surrounded mostly by high values, despite one less-similar neighbour. Next, hold the residual values and weights fixed, randomly permute the 36 values across cells, and recompute that local statistic many times; the observed value’s rank in this reference distribution is evidence about unusual local concentration, not proof of diffusion. Repeat the diagnostic under a defensible diagonal-weight rule, record which regions change classification, and account for multiple local tests. A local result remains descriptive unless treatment exposure, timing, interference, and a credible counterfactual support a causal spillover claim.

bootstrap-inference.Resample the data you have: Illustrative synthetic lab audit: suppose the control is set to n = 50 and B = 400, and the recorded bootstrap medians have a mean of 20.4 synthetic units with a sum of squared deviations of 806.4 synthetic-units². The bootstrap standard deviation is sqrt[806.4 ÷ (400 − 1)] = sqrt(2.020) = 1.42 synthetic units, so it measures replicate-to-replicate spread, not the standard deviation of the 50 original observations. To form a nearest-rank 95% percentile interval, sort all 400 medians: the lower rank is ceil(0.025 × 400) = 10 and the upper rank is ceil(0.975 × 400) = 390. If those ordered values are 17.8 and 23.6 synthetic units, respectively, the reported interval is 17.8–23.6 synthetic units. The observed median should be marked separately (for example, 19.6 synthetic units); it need not equal the bootstrap mean. Percentile interpolation conventions can move an endpoint slightly, so record the convention and check that increasing B leaves the trace and endpoints broadly stable. This is an illustrative computer calculation, not an observed wage estimate or a guarantee of 95% coverage.
bootstrap-inference.Read spread and intervals from the boots: Illustrative synthetic example: suppose an analyst estimates the median one-way commute time from seven sampled workers: 18, 21, 23, 24, 27, 32 and 46 minutes. The observed median is the fourth ordered value, 24 minutes. For each of B = 1,000 bootstrap replicates, draw seven worker records with replacement and recompute the median; do not divide by 1,000, because each resample still has n = 7. After sorting the medians, the lab’s linear-quantile rule places the lower endpoint at position 0.025(1,000 − 1) = 24.975, between the 25th and 26th ordered medians. If those are 18.4 and 18.5 minutes, the endpoint is 18.4 + 0.975(0.1) = 18.4975 minutes, or about 18.50 minutes. The upper position is 0.975(999) = 974.025; if the 975th and 976th values are 25.8 and 26.1 minutes, it is 25.8 + 0.025(0.3) = 25.8075, about 25.81 minutes. The approximate interval is therefore 18.50–25.81 minutes, conditional on workers being a defensible independent resampling unit. It describes sampling variation in the median, not the share of commuters whose true time lies in that range; clustered workplaces or survey weights require a different design.
bootstrap-inference.Match resampling to the data structure: Suppose an analyst has an illustrative, synthetic sample of five hourly wages (dollars per hour): 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16. The sample median is $14/hour. One bootstrap draw keeps size n = 5 but samples with replacement; for example, (13, 13, 15, 16, 16) has ordered middle value $15/hour, while (12, 12, 13, 14, 14) has median $13/hour. Repeating this operation B times creates a distribution of medians, not five new workers or a new wage survey. In a hypothetical run of B = 1,000, suppose the bootstrap medians have sample standard deviation $0.99/hour and percentile limits of $12/hour and $16/hour. Report the point estimate as $14/hour, the bootstrap SE as $0.99/hour, and the approximate percentile interval as [$12, $16] per hour. This interval describes sampling variation under the assumption that these observations reasonably represent independent draws from the target population; it is not a 95% probability statement about this fixed sample’s parameter. With n = 5, the replicate distribution is discrete and can have unreliable percentile coverage, so increasing B improves Monte Carlo smoothness but cannot repair poor representation or dependence.
bootstrap-inference.Choose a bootstrap model and inspect its: Illustrative synthetic example: suppose seven independently sampled workers have weekly earnings of 18, 21, 23, 24, 31, 45, and 60 hundred dollars. The observed median is the fourth ordered value, 24 hundred dollars per week. To make one bootstrap replicate, draw seven workers with replacement; a possible draw is 21, 21, 24, 31, 45, 45, 60, whose median is the fourth value, 31 hundred dollars per week. Another draw, 18, 18, 21, 23, 23, 24, 31, has median 23 hundred dollars per week. Repeating this procedure B times creates medians T*. If the resulting synthetic bootstrap distribution has a 2.5th percentile of 21 and a 97.5th percentile of 31 hundred dollars per week, the percentile interval is 21–31 hundred dollars per week; it describes an approximation to sampling uncertainty around the sample median, not a 95% probability that the fixed population median lies inside these particular endpoints. The inference also assumes the observed sample reasonably represents the target population. For a stratified or region-clustered wage survey, resample within strata or resample regions as designed; row-wise resampling can understate uncertainty.
bootstrap-inference.Connect bootstrap intervals to econometr: Consider an illustrative synthetic sample of six hourly wages, in dollars per hour: $18, $20, $21, $25, $31, and $40. The sample median is (21 + 25) / 2 = $23.00 per hour. One bootstrap resample must contain six draws with replacement; for example, [18, 21, 21, 31, 40, 40] has median (21 + 31) / 2 = $26.00 per hour. Another possible resample, [18, 18, 20, 21, 21, 25], has median (20 + 21) / 2 = $20.50 per hour. Repeating this operation B times gives a distribution of median estimates: its sample standard deviation is a bootstrap estimate of the median’s standard error, while its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form an approximate 95% percentile interval. That interval describes uncertainty under repeated samples resembling these six observed units; it is not a 95% probability that the fixed population median lies inside this particular interval. The interpretation also relies on the six wages being a defensible independent resampling unit; survey weights, strata, or worker clustering would require a design-matched procedure, and a small sample can make percentile limits unstable.
bootstrap-inference.Apply it to a regional wage comparison: To see why the statistic must be recomputed, consider an illustrative synthetic sample of six hourly wages in one region: $18, $20, $22, $27, $40, and $45. The observed median is ($22 + $27)/2 = $24.50 per hour. A bootstrap replicate draws six values with replacement; for example, $18, $22, $22, $40, $45, $45 sorts to $18, $22, $22, $40, $45, $45, giving T* = ($22 + $40)/2 = $31.00 per hour. Do this B times, store every T*, and calculate the sample standard deviation of those B medians as the bootstrap standard error: SE* = sqrt[Σ(T*_b − mean(T*))²/(B − 1)]. If a synthetic run produced SE* = $3.10 per hour and its central 95% percentile cutoffs were $19.20 and $31.80, report those as approximate uncertainty for the population median under the resampling assumptions—not as a 95% chance that this fixed interval contains the parameter. With only six workers, duplicated draws and unstable tails are expected; preserve survey strata or clusters rather than treating workers as independent when the design says otherwise.

statistical-power-planning.Start with a decision-relevant causal ta: Using the lab’s default settings as an explicitly synthetic planning example, let the minimum meaningful difference be δ = 0.8 outcome units, the outcome SD be σ = 4 units, and let n = 80 participants be assigned to each arm. For an equal-arm mean difference, the normal-approximation standard error is SE = σ√(2/n) = 4√(2/80) ≈ 0.632 units, so the specified effect is δ/SE ≈ 1.265 standard-error units. With a two-sided 5% cutoff, approximate power is 1 − Φ(1.960 − 1.265) + Φ(−1.960 − 1.265) ≈ 0.244, or 24.4%: this design often misses the threshold even when δ is the true planning alternative. Solving the same approximation for about 80% power gives n = ceil[2(1.960 + 0.842)²σ²/δ²] = ceil(392.4) = 393 per arm. If planners anticipate 20% loss to follow-up, a separate enrollment adjustment would be ceil(393/0.80) = 492 per arm, assuming losses are unrelated to assignment and outcomes; informative attrition or clustering requires a richer calculation. These are design scenarios, not observed findings or guarantees.
statistical-power-planning.Choose a precision target or a power tar: A useful sensitivity check is to ask how the required sample changes when the decision-relevant effect is smaller. Consider an illustrative synthetic planning scenario with independent equal arms, two-sided α = 0.05, 80% power, and σ = 4 outcome units. If the minimum worthwhile effect is δ = 1.2 units, the normal approximation gives n = 2(1.96 + 0.84)²(4²)/(1.2²) = 2(2.80)²(16)/1.44 ≈ 174.22, so round up to 175 participants per arm. If policy makers later judge δ = 0.6 units worthwhile, only the denominator changes: n ≈ 2(2.80)²(16)/0.36 = 696.89, requiring 697 per arm—four times as many because halving δ quadruples n. If anticipated follow-up retention is 85%, recruitment should be about 697/0.85 = 820 participants per arm, rounding upward, before allowing for clustering or unequal allocation. These values are synthetic planning scenarios, not observed results. The powerplan lab’s individual-level curve reflects the first calculation; clustered assignment, small-sample methods, or multiple primary outcomes require a design-specific adjustment rather than silently treating 820 people as 820 independent observations.
statistical-power-planning.Distinguish power from the minimum detec: Suppose the meaningful effect is a synthetic 0.8-unit increase in the outcome and the planning SD is 4 units. For a two-sided 5% test with 80% power, first calculate the analyzable participants needed per arm under the lab’s equal, independent-group normal approximation: n = 2(1.96 + 0.84)^2(4^2)/(0.8^2) = 2(2.80)^2(16)/0.64 = 392.0, so round up to 392 per arm (using the renderer’s more precise critical values gives about 393). That is an analysis requirement, not necessarily the number to recruit. If 15% attrition is anticipated and missingness does not differ in a way that changes the estimand, divide by the retained fraction: 393/0.85 = 462.35, hence recruit 463 per arm, or 926 total. The resulting claim is conditional: roughly 80% power applies if the SD, effect, test, and retention assumption are credible. Attrition can also reduce balance or change who is observed; differential follow-up may threaten validity rather than merely reduce power. With centre-level assignment, this individual-count calculation is insufficient: plan independent centres and their intracluster correlation instead.
statistical-power-planning.Account for assignment, clustering and a: Suppose, purely illustratively, an agency randomizes 16 employment centres—8 per arm—and recruits 18 participants per centre, for 144 participants per arm. If the outcome SD is 6 wage units and the intraclass correlation is 0.08, the equal-size design effect is 1 + (18 − 1)×0.08 = 2.36. The person-level count therefore corresponds to about 144/2.36 = 61.0 independent-person equivalents per arm. For a meaningful difference of 2.4 wage units, an approximate standard error for the arm difference is √(2×6²/61.0) = 1.09 wage units, giving a standardized signal of 2.4/1.09 = 2.20. With a two-sided 5% normal cutoff, approximate power is Φ(2.20 − 1.96) ≈ 0.60, not 80%. If 15% attrition is expected, dividing 144 by 0.85 gives 170 recruits per arm; rounding to 22 per centre gives 176 per arm, but this still leaves only eight independent centres in each arm. The calculation is synthetic and approximate: unequal centre sizes, selective attrition, small-cluster degrees of freedom, and covariate-adjusted analysis can change both the standard error and power, so the lab’s individual-level curve should not be read as this cluster design’s guarantee.
statistical-power-planning.Power cannot repair a weak design: Use the lab’s planning model to turn a policy threshold into a recruitment number, while keeping the comparison design separate from the arithmetic. Suppose an explicitly illustrative synthetic trial defines δ = £2 per worker per week as the smallest wage gain worth detecting, assumes an outcome standard deviation σ = £6 per week, uses a two-sided α = 0.05 test, and seeks 80% power. For two equal, independent arms, the normal-approximation calculation is n per arm ≈ 2[(1.959964 + 0.841621)^2 × 6^2] ÷ 2^2 = 141.28, so round up to 142 analysable workers in each arm; rounding down would miss the stated target under this model. If planners anticipate 15% attrition and assume it is unrelated to assignment and outcome, recruitment should be ceil(142 ÷ 0.85) = ceil(167.06) = 168 per arm. That adjustment protects the planned analysable count, but the assumption is substantive: differential attrition can bias the comparison even when nominal power is adequate. Cluster assignment, unequal arms, non-normal outcomes or a different estimand would invalidate this simple formula rather than merely require a larger integer.
statistical-power-planning.Plan a job-training evaluation: Consider a new synthetic planning scenario, not observed wage data: suppose the smallest worthwhile gain is δ = £0.80 per hour, the outcome SD is σ = £4.00 per hour, and an individually randomized study allocates n = 80 participants to each arm. Under the lab’s equal-size normal approximation, the standard error of the difference is SE = σ√(2/n) = 4√(2/80) ≈ £0.632 per hour. The standardized signal is δ/SE = 0.80/0.632 ≈ 1.26, so with a two-sided 5% cutoff the approximate power is P(Z > 1.96 − 1.26) + P(Z < −1.96 − 1.26) ≈ 0.244, or 24.4%. To target about 80% power for that same effect and spread, use n = ceil[2(1.959964 + 0.841621)²σ²/δ²] = ceil(392.4) = 393 per arm. This is a conditional design calculation: if assignment is by centre, replace this simple formula with a cluster-aware calculation, and inflate the 393 by the planned retention rate rather than treating it as the number recruited. Changing δ or σ changes the target quadratically, so reporting a sensitivity range is more honest than presenting 393 as a guarantee.

measurement-error-economics.Name the concept and the recorded variab: In an illustrative synthetic validation check for commuting time, suppose four people report 35, 52, 28 and 70 minutes, while a route-based comparison records 30, 50, 35 and 60 minutes for the same reference period. Define each discrepancy as reported minus comparison: +5, +2, −7 and +10 minutes. The mean signed discrepancy is (5 + 2 − 7 + 10) ÷ 4 = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 minutes, suggesting upward average reporting relative to this comparison. That conclusion is different from typical disagreement: the mean absolute error is (|5| + |2| + |−7| + |10|) ÷ 4 = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 minutes. Thus, opposite errors partly cancel in the signed mean even though individual records can differ by several minutes. Before applying a correction, check that both measures use the same start-and-end definition and time window; otherwise the discrepancy mixes measurement error with different estimands. Because the comparison route is itself a proxy and the four cases are a small, possibly selected validation sample, these figures are diagnostic evidence—not a universal correction or proof that either measure is true.
measurement-error-economics.Classical predictor error can flatten a: A repeated-measurement check can estimate reliability without pretending that one noisy record is the truth. In a synthetic commuting-time example, suppose two independent weekly reports measure the same latent time X: X₁* = X + u₁ and X₂* = X + u₂.
